soil-chem-135.title: Mica, the mineral that peels into thin elastic sheets
soil-chem-135.text: Mica comes apart in thin plates that bend and spring back. That property, perfect basal cleavage, defines the group: sheet silicate minerals whose crystals split easily along flat planes. They belong to the {{ref:soil-found-033}}, and the group holds 37 of them. Muscovite and the biotite series are common examples. Each layer is a sandwich, a pattern called TOT-c. Two tetrahedral sheets are bonded to one octahedral sheet between them. Only interlayer cations, positively charged ions, hold the layers together, and weakly, hence the cleavage. In most micas aluminium replaces one in four silicon ions. That swap leaves each layer with a negative charge, which interlayer sodium, potassium or calcium ions neutralize. Dioctahedral micas have a gibbsite-like aluminium sheet. Trioctahedral ones have a brucite-like sheet of magnesium or ferrous iron. Mica is common in igneous and metamorphic rocks and appears as small flakes in some sedimentary rocks. Very fine-grained, variable 'clay micas' include {{ref:soil-chem-094}}, which is short of potassium between its layers. Weathering turns muscovite into this clay and, together with feldspars, into kaolin minerals such as dickite.
